title: Trash Fees and Smart Bins
inOneSentence: How Seoul charges households for trash: priced bags for general trash since 1995, and shared smart bins that weigh food waste and bill each household for it.
background: Since 1995, everyone in Korea, Seoul included, has paid for general trash by buying official priced bags. General trash means anything that is not recycling or food waste, which are kept separate. The more trash you throw out, the more bags you have to buy, so people have a reason to throw out less. This kind of system is called pay as you throw, and Korea's version is the one other countries usually point to.

Food waste goes into shared smart bins instead. A resident taps a household RFID card on the bin, the lid opens, the bin weighs what goes in, and that household is billed for the weight. The 3D diagram on the slide walks through these three steps. The 4.2 kg on the bin's display is only an example.

There is a reward too. A household that cuts its food waste by 10 to 30% compared with the same period a year earlier can earn up to 5,000 points in each evaluation period, worth about ₩5,000. The separated food waste is turned into animal feed, compost and biogas.

The results are on the slide. The bag fees cut trash by about 8% in 1995 and 11% by 1996, both compared with 1994. Seoul Solution warns that the 1995 number may be too high, because many people threw out large items for free that year, so the 1996 number is the more reliable one. For food waste, Korean agency reporting from December 2013 gives a 10 to 30% drop, and a comparison table on the same site gives 9 to 31% for the weighing bins.

New York has made curbside composting mandatory, and buildings can be fined $25 to $100 if they have 1 to 8 units, and $100 to $300 if they have 9 or more. But New York's brown bins don't weigh anything and there is no reward, so a household never learns how much food it throws out. Seoul's bin gives each household its own number every time. That gap becomes the first idea New York could borrow, on slide 19.

explainSimply: It works like a water or electric meter. You pay for what you use, and the bill shows you how much that was. Seoul does this for food scraps. The bin is the meter, and every time you use it, your household sees its own number.

questions.q: How does the bin know whose food waste it is?
questions.a: Each household has an RFID card, a chip card like a building key fob. You tap it on the bin, the lid opens, and the bin weighs what you drop in. Your household is then billed for that weight.

questions.q: Doesn't charging for trash make people dump it illegally?
questions.a: That's a common worry with any trash fee. Korea backs its fees with fines of up to ₩100,000 for breaking the rules. My sources don't measure illegal dumping, so I can't give a number for it. What they do show is that trash went down 11% by 1996 after the fees started.

questions.q: Is the 9 to 31% drop really because of the bins, or because of other things like the points or the bag fees?
questions.a: Korean agency reporting from December 2013 gives a 10 to 30% drop, and a comparison table on the same site gives 9 to 31% for the RFID bins. My sources don't explain how it was measured, so I treat it as a reported range and don't say the bin alone caused it.

questions.q: Could New York do this?
questions.a: New York already has the rule and the fines for composting. What it doesn't have is a bin that tells each household how much it threw out, or a reward for cutting back. New York already requires refuse rooms in apartment buildings, so bins that weigh food waste could go there. This is idea 1 on slide 19.

questions.q: How much is ₩490 in US dollars?
questions.a: My sources give the price in won only, and exchange rates change, so I'd check a current rate before giving a dollar figure.

dontSay: Don't say every household in Seoul uses a weighing bin. The dossier describes shared smart bins but gives no figure for how many homes have them.
Don't present the 4.2 kg on the diagram as a real measurement. It's an example.
Don't lean on the 8% drop for 1995. Seoul Solution itself says it may be too high, so use the 11% for 1996.
Don't mix up the two ranges. Use 9 to 31% for the RFID bins and 10 to 30% for the points rule.
Don't use the recycling figures (recycling up more than 30%, about 70% of household waste recycled). They come from one source and aren't measured from the same starting point.
Don't say New Yorkers pay for food waste by weight. New York fines buildings that don't separate it, and nobody is charged by weight.
Don't call Korea's system the strictest in the world as if it were a measured fact.

nycLink: New York uses the stick for composting. It's mandatory, and fines came back on January 1, 2026. But the bins give no feedback and there's no reward, and organics were only about 2.4% of residential waste collected in 2025. Seoul's weighing bin adds the two things New York is missing, which becomes idea 1 on slide 19. It also fits the title of the talk, since Seoul pairs a stick (paying by weight) with a carrot (points).

title: From Landfill to Park
inOneSentence: How Seoul turned Nanjido, its old garbage mountain, into World Cup Park, and how New York is doing the same thing at Freshkills.
background: Nanjido (nahn-jee-doh) was an island in the Han River. Work on an embankment joining it to the mainland began in January 1977, and in 1978 it became Seoul's official dump. It was picked because it was easy to reach and far from downtown.

Over about 15 years the trash piled up into two mounds about 90 m high, roughly as tall as a 30-story building. Korea had no modern system for landfill gas or leachate at the time. Leachate is the dirty liquid that drains out of buried trash. Rotting trash makes methane, and the site gave off methane and toxic gases.

Planning to fix the site started in 1991. In 1993 the city decided to close the dump and stabilize the ground (some sources say dumping ended in 1992). The 3D diagram shows the general idea of the fix: a sealed cap over the trash, wells that collect the gas, and a park on top. The gas is now captured and used. Construction ran from 1996 to 2002, and the site opened as World Cup Park for the 2002 FIFA World Cup. The two mounds became Haneul Park (hah-nool, meaning sky) and Noeul Park (no-ool).

In 2012 the Seoul Energy Dream Center, Korea's first zero-energy public building, opened on the same ground (slide 10). The old trash can't carry a building's weight, so the center stands on piles that reach down to solid ground.

New York is doing the same thing at Freshkills Park on Staten Island. Fresh Kills was once the world's largest landfill, and it is becoming a park of about 2,200 acres that opens in phases. The two cities reached the same answer on their own, on roughly the same timeline, so this slide presents them as equals.

questions.a: It's pulled out through wells in the mounds and used. My sources don't say exactly what it's used for, so I wouldn't say it makes electricity or heats homes.

questions.q: How does Freshkills compare with Nanjido?
questions.a: Fresh Kills on Staten Island was once the world's largest landfill, and it's becoming a park of about 2,200 acres. Seoul's park opened in 2002, and Freshkills is still opening in phases. The two cities came to the same idea on their own, on roughly the same timeline.

title: The 2026 Landfill Ban
inOneSentence: Since January 1, 2026, Seoul and its region can't bury raw household trash, but they didn't build enough incinerators first, so some trash is now sent to other cities.
background: In 2021, a law banned direct landfilling of household waste in Seoul, Incheon and Gyeonggi, the area together called the capital region. Direct landfilling means burying raw household trash. Under the ban, trash has to be burned or processed first. The law gave the region a five-year grace period to get ready.

During those five years, local governments mostly did not add incinerator capacity. One news report says they effectively neglected it. Seoul still runs only four public incinerators, in Gangnam, Mapo, Nowon and Yangcheon, and most of them are 20 to 30 or more years old. The ban still started on schedule on January 1, 2026, with no emergency delay.

From January to June 2026, Seoul's privately handled household waste reached 457 tons a day, a 3.2-fold rise. Public incineration went up by only 80 tons (from 1,921 to 2,001 tons). As a result, much of the trash went to private companies, and some of it left the region. Gangdong district ships waste to private incinerators in Cheonan and Sejong, and Gangnam district plans to send waste to Cheongju. On the map, the straight-line distances from central Seoul are about 85 km to Cheonan, 110 km to Cheongju and 125 km to Sejong. Seoul Economic Daily reported that some trash travels about 130 km, which would be the distance by road.

The cities receiving the trash are pushing back. Operators in Cheongju agreed not to bid on contracts from Seoul, Incheon or Gyeonggi through the end of next year. This is an environmental justice problem, because the trash ends up in communities that didn't make it. Amendments to the Wastes Control Act are pending in the National Assembly with no clear timing, and the nearby city of Seongnam is building a new 500-ton-a-day incinerator to replace an old one.

The slide ends with a question for the class. New York's Local Law 97 fines buildings that go over their emissions caps, and about 63% of covered buildings are projected to miss their 2030 caps without further action. Seoul set its deadline before the incinerators were ready. The question is whether New York's retrofit workers and supply chain can keep up with what LL97 asks for. This is where you stop talking and let the class answer.

questions.q: Isn't burning trash bad for the climate too?
questions.a: Burning trash does release greenhouse gases, and one of my sources studies emissions from Seoul's incinerators. Buried raw trash also rots and gives off methane, as it did at Nanjido. My sources don't spell out why the ban was passed. My point on this slide is about timing. The replacement wasn't ready when the ban started.

questions.q: 457 tons a day went to private companies, but public incineration only rose 80 tons. Do those numbers add up?
questions.a: The 457 is tons a day for January to June 2026. My source doesn't give a time period for the 80-ton rise (1,921 to 2,001 tons), so I don't compare the two directly. Both numbers show public incinerators took on little while private handling jumped.

questions.q: Is 130 km the actual distance?

questions.q: What does a trash problem in Seoul have to do with LL97?
questions.a: Both are hard rules with a deadline. LL97 fines buildings $268 for each ton over their cap, and about 63% of covered buildings are projected to miss their 2030 caps without further action. Seoul's rule came before its incinerators did. If New York's retrofit workers and supply chain can't keep up, LL97 could hit a similar wall, and that's the question I want the class to discuss.

Don't bring back the old closing slogan about a ban being only a deadline. Ask the question on the slide instead.

title: Restoring Cheonggyecheon
inOneSentence: Seoul removed an elevated highway and uncovered the stream buried under it, and the area gained wildlife, cleaner air and cooler temperatures without the traffic jams people expected.
background: Cheonggyecheon (chung-gyeh-chun) is a stream in central Seoul. It was buried under an elevated highway that carried about 168,000 vehicles a day. From 2003 to 2005, Seoul took the highway down and opened the stream back up. Uncovering a buried stream like this is called daylighting. The project cost about US$281 million and restored about 5.8 km (3.6 miles) of corridor.

Wildlife came back. A Landscape Architecture Foundation case study reports that between 2003 and 2008 plant species went from 62 to 308, insects from 15 to 192, birds from 6 to 36 and fish from 4 to 25. You'll often see a "639% increase in biodiversity" quoted. It's an overall index, so it can't be read as a species count. The counts for each group are safer to give. Plants alone went up about 397%, so there were about five times as many plant species.

The air got cleaner and the area got cooler. Small-particle air pollution fell from 74 to 48 micrograms per cubic meter, about 35% less. The highest cooling estimate says the corridor is 3.3 to 5.9°C cooler than a parallel road 4 to 7 blocks away. Other sources find a smaller effect. WWF says 3 to 4°C cooler than areas 400 m away. Metropolis says the area went from 2.2°C above the Seoul average to 1.3°C above. A peer-reviewed study that pulled many studies together is the most careful source, and it found lower daily average temperatures within about 300 m of the stream.

Many people expected traffic chaos when the highway closed, and it didn't happen. In general, when road space is taken away, some drivers take other routes, some switch to transit, and some trips stop happening. Planners call this reduced demand. It's the opposite of induced demand, where new roads fill up with new traffic. Bus ridership in the corridor rose 15.1% from 2003 to 2008, but Seoul's big 2004 bus reform happened at the same time, so the stream shouldn't get all the credit.

For New York, this is evidence for the debates over the Brooklyn-Queens Expressway (BQE), the Cross Bronx Expressway and the Gowanus Expressway. The High Line reused an old rail line, so no drivers lost a road. Cheonggyecheon removed a busy road that drivers used every day, and the gridlock people predicted did not happen.

questions.q: Where did all the cars go?
questions.a: In general, when road space is removed, some drivers take other routes, some switch to buses or the subway, and some trips just stop happening. Planners call this reduced demand. Bus ridership in the corridor rose 15.1% from 2003 to 2008, but the 2004 bus reform happened at the same time and deserves part of the credit.

questions.q: Is the stream natural? Where does the water come from, and what does it cost to keep up?

questions.q: Why not use the 639% figure? It sounds impressive.
questions.a: It's an overall index, so it can't be read as a species count. The counts for each group are clearer. Plants went from 62 to 308 species, about 397% more. Fish went from 4 to 25, birds from 6 to 36 and insects from 15 to 192.

questions.q: How much cooler is it really?
questions.a: It depends on what you compare it with. The highest estimate says 3.3 to 5.9°C cooler than a parallel road 4 to 7 blocks away. WWF says 3 to 4°C cooler than areas 400 m away. A peer-reviewed study that pulled many studies together is the most careful source, and it found lower daily average temperatures within about 300 m of the stream.

questions.q: Could New York take down the BQE or the Cross Bronx?
questions.a: Those are live debates, and there are proposals to cap parts of the Cross Bronx. Cheonggyecheon shows that removing a busy elevated highway didn't cause the gridlock people predicted. Every city's road network is different, so the result here could be different.

dontSay: Don't present the 639% as a species count. It's an overall index.
Don't give 3.3 to 5.9°C as the only cooling number. It's the highest estimate, so give the range.
Don't give the stream all the credit for the 15.1% bus rise. The 2004 bus reform happened at the same time.
Don't say traffic got better everywhere. The sources say the predicted gridlock didn't happen.
Don't call the pollution PM10 or PM2.5. The dossier only says small-particle pollution.
Don't add history the dossier doesn't cover, like when the stream was first covered or who led the project, unless you check it first.
Don't call the 168,000 "cars." The sources count vehicles.

terms.meaning: Uncovering a stream that had been buried in a pipe or under a road, so it runs in the open again.
A highway raised on columns above the street.
Micrograms per cubic meter: how many millionths of a gram of particles float in one cubic meter of air.
Tiny bits of dust, soot and smoke in the air, much of it from traffic, that can get deep into your lungs.
When road space is taken away, some car trips stop happening, so traffic doesn't simply move onto nearby streets.
The opposite effect. New or wider roads attract new traffic and fill up again.
A study that gathers the published research on a topic and compares it using set rules. It is usually more careful than relying on one study.

nycLink: New York's High Line reused an old rail line, which was the easy case because no drivers lost a road. Seoul removed a highway in heavy daily use, and the gridlock people predicted didn't happen. That's useful evidence for New York's debates over the BQE, the Cross Bronx and the Gowanus, and it becomes the fifth idea on slide 19.

title: A Stream and a Highway
seoul: Cheonggyecheon today, an open stream with planted banks and walkways in central Seoul. From 2003 to 2005, an elevated highway carrying about 168,000 vehicles a day was taken down to uncover it.
nyc: The Cross Bronx Expressway, still open to traffic. There are proposals to cap parts of it, which means building a deck over the highway, often with a park on top.
why: Seoul removed its highway and got a stream back. The Cross Bronx is still there, so the pair shows the choice New York is still debating.
